fetched_contents.text: Etiology of bacterial pneumonia and multi-drug resistance pattern among pneumonia suspected patients in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background Bacterial pneumonia can affect all age groups, but people with weakened immune systems, young children, and the elderly are at a higher risk. Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are the most common causative agents of pneumonia, and they have developed high MDR in recent decades in Ethiopia. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the pooled prevalence of bacterial pneumonia and multidrug resistance in Ethiopia. Methods The articles were searched extensively in the electronic databases and grey literature using entry terms or phrases. Studies meeting the eligibility criteria were extracted in MS Excel and exported for statistical analysis into STATA version 14 software. The pooled prevalence of bacterial pneumonia and multidrug resistance were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed by using the I2 value. Publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and Egger’s test. A sensitivity analysis was done to assess the impact of a single study on the pooled effect size. Result Of the 651 studies identified, 87 were eligible for qualitative analysis, of which 11 were included in the meta-analysis consisting of 1154 isolates. The individual studies reported prevalence of bacterial pneumonia ranging from 6.19 to 46.3%. In this systematic review and metanalysis, the pooled prevalence of bacterial pneumonia in Ethiopia was 37.17% (95% CI 25.72–46.62), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 98.4%, p < 0.001) across the studies. The pooled prevalence of multidrug resistance in bacteria isolated from patients with pneumonia in Ethiopia was 67.73% (95% CI: 57.05–78.40). The most commonly isolated bacteria was Klebsiella pneumoniae, with pooled prevalence of 21.97% (95% CI 16.11–27.83), followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae, with pooled prevalence of 17.02% (95% CI 9.19–24.86), respectively. Conclusion The pooled prevalence of bacterial isolates from bacterial pneumonia and their multidrug resistance were high among Ethiopian population. The initial empirical treatment of these patients remains challenging because of the strikingly high prevalence of antimicrobial resistance. fetched_contents.text: Bacterial etiology, antimicrobial resistance and factors associated with community acquired pneumonia among adult hospitalized patients in Southwest Ethiopia Abstract Background and Objectives: Antibiotic resistance is a significant problem that restricts the options for treating bacterial pneumonia. This research aimed to determine the bacterial causes of pneumonia and antibiotic resistance among hospitalized patients in southwest Ethiopia. Materials and Methods: We collected and analyzed 150 sputum samples from individuals with community-acquired pneumonia from April 1st to October 30th, 2019. Standard bacteriological procedures were used to identify the bacteria. Kirby Bauer’s disk diffusion method was used to assess the bacteria’s susceptibility patterns. Production of carbapenemase and extended-spectrum-lactamase were confirmed phenotypically. Odds ratios and the chi-square test were computed. Results: On the whole, bacterial pathogens were verified in 50% of the sputum samples. The predominant bacterial isolates were Klebsiella species, followed by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae. About 77.5% of isolates were multidrug resistant. Moreover, 40.5% and 10.8% of the isolates were ESBL and carbapenemase producers, respectively. Aging, tobacco smoking, previous history of pneumonia, heart disease, and chronic respiratory disease had association with sputum culture-positivity. Conclusion: As a result, it is important to regularly monitor the bacterial etiologies and their patterns of resistance. Additionally, sociodemographic and clinical characteristics should all be taken into account while managing patients with pneumonia empirically in this context. This includes lung abscesses, acute bronchitis, and pneumonia (1, 2). One of the main reasons for hospitalization and death worldwide is pneumonia (3). Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is an infection obtained after at least 48 hours of hospitalization, whereas community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is an infection acquired outside of the hospital setting. Numerous microbes, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi, can cause it (4, 5). According to many studies, a variety of factors, including an increase in patient age, the existence of comorbidities, cigarette and alcohol use, and chronic malnutrition, put the population at risk for pneumonia (6, 7). Additionally, the use of recent antibiotics, corticosteroids, and structural lung disease are risk factors for gram-negative pneumonia infection (8). The commonest etiologies of pneumonia are viruses to which antibiotics are often unnecessarily prescribed (9, 10). Additionally, there can be significant differences in the microbial flora and antimicrobial resistance patterns between and within nations, regions, hospitals, ICUs within hospitals, and specimen sources through different means (11, 12). As a result, accurate diagnosis of the causes of pneumonia and knowledge of their susceptibility patterns will help to reduce the need for unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions, which could help fight antimicrobial resistance (9, 10, 12). In Ethiopia, bacterial etiologies of community-acquired pneumonia from outpatients, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella species, S. aureus, H. influenzae, Pseudomonas species and Acinetobacter species are frequently isolated with different levels of resistance for different antibiotics (13–16). However, there is no published data on the bacteriological profiles and patterns of antibiotic resistance among hospitalized patients in Ethiopia with community-acquired pneumonia in general and in the research context. Thus, this study was conducted to identify bacterial etiologies and associated antibiotic resistance patterns among hospitalized patients with community-acquired pneumonia at Jimma Medical Center (JMC), Jimma, Ethiopia. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study design and setting. From April 1 to October 30, 2019, a cross-sectional study was carried out at Jimma Medical Centre in Jimma Town, southwest Ethiopia. With a bed capacity of 800, it is the only teaching and referral hospital in the country’s southwest. With a catchment population of more than 20 million people, it serves over 15,000 inpatients, 160,000 outpatient attendants, 11,000 emergency cases, and 4500 deliveries annually. Source population. All adult patients clinically diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia at Jimma Medical Center. Study population. All adult hospitalized patients diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia at Jimma Medical Center from April 1 to October 30, 2019. Inclusioncriteria. All adult hospitalized patients diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia agreed to the study and provided written informed consent. Exclusion criteria. The study excluded patients who were seriously unwell, known cases of tuberculosis, a history of hospital admission in the previous two weeks, those who were admitted to the hospital for at least 48 hours prior to data collection and who were unable to provide adequate sputum sample. Finally, a total of 150 study participants who provided good quality of sputum (<10 SECs per LPF and >25 PMNs per LPF on gram stain), recruited using the purposive sampling technique (17). Data and sample collection. By using a face-to-face administered structured questionnaire, socio-demographic traits, clinical, and behavioral aspects of the patients were collected. fetched_contents.text: Magnitude and associated factors of pneumonia among under-five children visiting outpatient department of public hospitals in Jigjiga city, Somali region, Ethiopia in 2024 Abstract Introduction Pneumonia is a common and severe inflammatory condition affecting children under five years old, particularly in Southern Asia and Africa. In Ethiopia, approximately 3.37 million children under five contract pneumonia each year. Pneumonia is major health problem in Ethiopia, and studying it can help improve child health outcomes. Objective This study aimed to estimate the magnitude and associated factors of pneumonia among under-five children visiting outpatient departments of public hospitals in Jigjiga city, Ethiopia. Methodology A cross-sectional study was conducted at two public hospitals in Jigjiga city from March 15 to April 15, 2024, 2024. A systematic random sampling was implied to collect primary data from 341 under-five children visiting outpatient departments. The data was entered and cleaned using Epi data version 3.1 and exported to SPSS version 20 for analysis. Multivariable binary logistic regression models were employed to analyse the data. Result The study revealed that the magnitude of pneumonia was 33.4% and the risk factors for under-five pneumonia were identified. Children carried on their mothers back during cooking (AOR: 4.32, 95%CI: 1.67–11.1), with history of house hold ARTI (AOR: 4.39, 95%CI: 1.49–12.6), partially vaccinated (AOR: 5.33, 95%CI: 1.09–26.07), unvaccinated (AOR: 7.18, 95%CI: 1.18–44.4), had diarrhea (AOR: 3.61, 95%CI: 1.8–9.44), being female (AOR: 2.6, 95%CI: 1.18–5.77) were significantly associate with under five pneumonias. Conclusion This study found a very high number of young children with pneumonia. Children, who weren’t fully vaccinated, were exposed to cooking smoke, household members with respiratory infections, had diarrhea, or were girls all had a much higher risk. This suggests that getting kids fully vaccinated and reducing indoor air pollution are key ways to bring down pneumonia rates. It is particularly prevalent among children who are under the age of five [1]. Children under the age of five are estimated to experience an incidence rate of 0.29 episodes of pneumonia per child-year. This translates to approximately 151.8 million cases occurring each year in developing countries while developed countries record only 4 million cases [2]. Globally, there are over 1,400 instances of pneumonia per 100,000 children, with Southern Asia and Africa experiencing the highest number of cases. Out of all the continents, Africa has the most significant incidence and severe cases of pneumonia, with a yearly occurrence of 35 million pneumonia cases among children under the age of five [3]. This region, especially East Africa, faces a significant burden, with pneumonia prevalence reaching as high as 34% [4]. Particularly in Ethiopia, around 3,370,000 children under the age of five contract pneumonia each year [5]. Around half of pneumonia-related deaths occur in just five heavily populated and economically poorest countries: India, Nigeria, Democratic Republic of Congo, Pakistan, and Ethiopia [6]. Consequently, Ethiopia ranks fifth among the top 15 countries with the highest mortality rate for children under the age of five due to clinical pneumonia, with 62 deaths per 1000 children [7]. According to a recent systematic meta-analysis, the overall prevalence of pneumonia among children under the age of five in Ethiopia is 20.68% [8]. Likewise, pneumonia is the most commonly occurring acute respiratory infection, accounting for 20% of cases, among children aged two months to five years in urban areas of the Oromia national regional state. However, the scarcity of data on pneumonia rates in children under five in the Somali regional state hinders the accurate assessment of the prevalence of this respiratory condition [9]. Astoundingly, almost half of all pneumonia deaths can be attributed to the detrimental impact of air pollution. It is crucial to recognize that indoor air pollution poses a more significant risk to the lives of children worldwide than outdoor air pollution [12, 13]. Studies have shown that various factors, including outdoor air pollutants, diurnal temperature range, tree and weed pollen, as well as human rhinovirus and influenza virus, have significant impacts on the respiratory systems of children [14]. Branch report on multidrug resistance and resistance patterns

The evidence points to a high overall burden of multidrug resistance (MDR) among bacterial isolates from pneumonia cases in Ethiopia, but the reported fraction of isolates with MDR is not uniform across all studies and is influenced by region, pathogen type, and study design. A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that the pooled prevalence of MDR in bacteria isolated from patients with pneumonia in Ethiopia was 67.73% (95% CI: 57.05–78.40) [N2-R1]. A separate systematic review of Ethiopia-wide MDR prevalence found an overall pooled prevalence of 70.5%, with Sidama region at the highest reported MDR level (81.7%) and Tigray at the lowest (51.1%) [N2-R2]. These regional differences suggest that MDR prevalence is not homogeneous across Ethiopia and may vary substantially depending on the local study population.

The most common bacteria isolated in the included studies were Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae, with Klebsiella pneumoniae having the highest pooled prevalence at 21.97% (95% CI 16.11–27.83) and Streptococcus pneumoniae at 17.02% (95% CI 9.19–24.86) [N1-F1]. This is important because resistance patterns are pathogen-specific: the review notes that multidrug resistance is especially notable for the most common causative agents of pneumonia in Ethiopia, and that S. pneumoniae, K. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and P. aeruginosa have developed high MDR in recent decades in the country [N1-F1]. The evidence also implies that resistance is not confined to one region or one pathogen type; rather, the same high MDR burden is reported across different isolates from pneumonia-suspected patients.

On resistance genes and patterns, the evidence is thinner and more indirect than the prevalence estimates. The strongest direct evidence is that multidrug resistance is defined as resistance to at least three or more classes of antibiotics, and the review explicitly notes the presence of extensive drug resistance (XDR) and pan-drug resistance (PDR) as more extreme forms of resistance [N1-F1]. A separate study from southwest Ethiopia reported that 77.5% of isolates were multidrug resistant, with 40.5% ESBL producers and 10.8% carbapenemase producers [N5-F2]. This regional study provides a concrete example of resistance patterns: carbapenemase and extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) production are both important resistance mechanisms, and their co-occurrence is associated with very high MDR levels [N5-F2]. However, the evidence does not provide a full catalog of resistance genes across all regions; the regional differences reported are mainly in prevalence rather than in gene-specific profiles.

Regional variation in resistance is supported by the Ethiopia-wide meta-analysis and the systematic review of MDR prevalence, which found substantial regional heterogeneity in MDR prevalence, with Sidama having the highest and Tigray the lowest reported MDR [N2-R1][N2-R2]. The evidence also implies that pathogen-type variation contributes to resistance patterns: Klebsiella species, S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, and P. aeruginosa were the dominant isolates in the pooled analysis, and these were the main pathogens reported as having high MDR prevalence [N1-F1]. In other words, the resistance burden is not only regional but also tied to which bacterial species are more common in a given area.

Overall, the evidence supports a strong conclusion: multidrug resistance is common in Ethiopian pneumonia-associated bacteria, with MDR prevalence around 67–70% nationally [N2-R1][N2-R2], but the exact fraction of isolates with MDR varies by region, study design, and pathogen type. The available evidence is strongest for prevalence and broad resistance mechanisms, but it is weaker for gene-level details and precise regional patterns beyond the large regional contrasts provided in the systematic reviews [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].
node_outputs.N8:
Branch report on regional pneumonia prevalence across Ethiopia

The evidence indicates substantial regional variation in pneumonia prevalence across Ethiopia, but the regional estimates are not uniform and are influenced by age group, setting, and study design. A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that the pooled prevalence of bacterial pneumonia in Ethiopia was 37.17% (95% CI 25.72–46.62), with substantial heterogeneity across studies (I² = 98.4%) [N1-F1]. This pooled estimate is important because it shows that individual studies vary widely, and that regional differences are not captured simply by a single national average [N1-F1].

Regional prevalence estimates in the evidence are explicit but uneven. The review reports that individual studies reported bacterial pneumonia prevalence ranging from 6.19% to 46.3%, with specific examples from Addis Ababa and Dessie [N1-R1]. A more detailed regional context comes from the pooled analysis, which found that southern Ethiopia had a reported prevalence of 42.9% and central Ethiopia 32.1%, with S. pneumoniae and K. pneumoniae as predominant isolates in those regions [N1-F1]. This suggests that pneumonia prevalence is higher in some regions than in others, and that the difference is not trivial. The review also notes that prevalence varied by setting and by age group, with the positive culture rate being slightly higher in women and higher prevalence rates observed in age groups greater than or equal to 45 years [N1-F1]. This is important because it shows that prevalence is not only regional but also age-dependent.

The evidence also includes pneumonia prevalence studies from specific regions and settings. A systematic meta-analysis on under-five children reported an overall prevalence of 20.68% for pneumonia among children under five in Ethiopia, with a wide range from 4.1% to 39.6% [N1-R4]. This range reflects substantial variation by study population and setting. Another regional report on under-five children in Jigjiga city, Somali region, Ethiopia, found a pneumonia prevalence of 33.4% [N6-F3]. A study from Wondo Genet district, Sidama Zone, Ethiopia, focused on children aged 2–59 months and aimed to determine prevalence and associated factors [N6-R3]. A study in Awi Zone, Northwest Ethiopia, similarly aimed to assess community-acquired pneumonia and its associated factors among under-five children [N4-R3]. These examples show that regional studies are common in Ethiopia, but they also show that the age groups and settings being studied differ: one study is focused on under-five children, another on hospitalized adults, and another on hospitalized patients in a referral setting [N6-F3][N5-F2].

Confidence in regional estimates is limited by substantial heterogeneity and study design differences. The pooled bacterial pneumonia analysis had I² = 98.4%, indicating very high heterogeneity across studies, which makes direct comparison of regional prevalence estimates difficult [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis also notes that the included studies were heterogeneous in design, and that pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model to account for this heterogeneity [N1-F1]. The systematic review on under-five children reported an overall prevalence of 20.68% with a wide range, which again underscores that regional estimates can vary widely depending on the population and setting [N1-R4]. In addition, the evidence from the study on hospitalized adult patients in southwest Ethiopia shows that the prevalence of bacterial etiology was 50% among sputum samples, with Klebsiella species as the most common isolate [N5-F2]. This indicates that hospitalized adult pneumonia studies may report different prevalence than studies in outpatient or under-five settings [N5-F2].

In summary, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: pneumonia prevalence in Ethiopia varies substantially by region, age group, and setting, with some studies reporting as low as 6.19% and as high as 46.3% [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The regional differences are real, but the available evidence is also highly heterogeneous, with substantial I² heterogeneity and a wide range of prevalence estimates across studies [N1-F1][N1-R4]. Therefore, regional estimates should be interpreted cautiously and should not be treated as exact or comparable without further methodological standardization [N1-F1][N6-F3].

Branch report on study comparability and regional bias

The evidence indicates that the studies included in the regional pneumonia and MDR literature differ substantially in diagnostic methods, sampling settings, and study design, which limits comparability. A systematic review on bacterial pneumonia and multidrug resistance in Ethiopia reported that the included studies varied widely, with prevalence estimates ranging from 6.19% to 46.3% [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This wide range suggests that study design and sampling strategy are major sources of heterogeneity. The same review also noted that the pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model because of substantial heterogeneity across studies, with I² = 98.4% [N1-F1]. That level of heterogeneity strongly implies that the studies are not comparable in a straightforward way and that regional comparisons must be made with caution.

Diagnostic methods differ across studies. The evidence includes both pneumonia prevalence studies and studies on bacterial etiology and antimicrobial resistance. For example, one study on hospitalized adult patients in southwest Ethiopia used standard bacteriological procedures and Kirby Bauer’s disk diffusion method, with phenotypic confirmation of carbapenemase and extended-spectrum-lactamase production [N5-F2]. Another study on bacterial pneumonia used a systematic review and meta-analysis approach, which synthesized prevalence data from multiple studies but did not itself perform direct laboratory testing [N1-F1]. A separate systematic review on under-five children estimated pneumonia prevalence using a meta-analysis of observational studies, including those from outpatient departments and hospitals [N6-F3]. These different diagnostic approaches—direct microbiological testing, systematic review of prevalence data, and meta-analysis of observational studies—make direct comparison difficult because they measure different things and use different levels of evidence.

Sampling bias from urban versus rural or referral versus primary care settings is also evident. The evidence includes studies from Addis Ababa [N1-R1], Dessie [N1-R1], southwest Ethiopia [N5-F2], and Jigjiga city in the Somali region [N6-F3]. These locations differ in setting and population mix. The study from southwest Ethiopia was conducted at a teaching and referral hospital in Jimma, which serves a large catchment population and is therefore likely to include more severe or hospitalized cases [N5-F2]. In contrast, the study on under-five children in Jigjiga city was conducted in public hospitals and focused on outpatient departments [N6-F3]. A study from Awi Zone, Northwest Ethiopia, also focused on under-five children in a regional setting [N4-R3]. These examples show that prevalence can vary because hospitalized patients, outpatient children, and community settings may have different risk profiles, different access to care, and different disease severity distributions.

Limitations in comparing regional estimates are therefore considerable. First, the high I² heterogeneity across bacterial pneumonia studies makes it difficult to compare regional estimates directly [N1-F1]. Second, the prevalence range from 6.19% to 46.3% shows that the same region can produce very different results depending on the study population and methodology [N1-R1][N1-F1]. Third, the evidence suggests that studies differ by age group and setting: some focus on under-five children, others on hospitalized adults, and others on pneumonia-suspected patients [N1-F1][N5-F2][N6-F3]. Fourth, the evidence also notes that the pooled prevalence of bacterial pneumonia was calculated using a random-effects model, which is appropriate when heterogeneity is high, but it does not eliminate the need for cautious interpretation [N1-F1]. Finally, the evidence on MDR prevalence also shows regional differences, with Sidama reported at the highest MDR level and Tigray at the lowest [N2-R2], but those differences may reflect sampling bias, regional variation in antibiotic use, and differences in the pathogens studied rather than a single underlying rate [N2-R2].

Overall, the evidence supports a strong conclusion: regional pneumonia and MDR studies in Ethiopia are not directly comparable because they differ in diagnostic methods, sampling settings, and study design [N1-F1][N5-F2][N6-F3]. The wide prevalence range and high heterogeneity mean that regional estimates should be interpreted cautiously, and comparisons should be made only when studies are methodologically similar and the populations studied are comparable [N1-F1][N1-R1].

Branch report on regional variation in risk factors and severity

The evidence suggests that risk factors for pneumonia and pneumonia outcomes vary by region in Ethiopia, but the available data are mixed in detail and are mainly drawn from under-five children and hospitalized adult studies. A systematic review on under-five children reported that pneumonia prevalence among children under five in Ethiopia was 20.68% overall, with a wide range from 4.1% to 39.6% [N1-R4]. This wide range already implies that regional variation is real, but the evidence also indicates that risk factors differ by region and by study population.

Among the risk factors reported in the evidence, poverty-related factors are prominent. The evidence notes that pneumonia deaths are strongly linked to poverty-related factors, including inadequate nutrition, lack of access to safe water and sanitation, indoor air pollution, and limited healthcare access [N7-R1]. The same source emphasizes that almost half of all pneumonia deaths can be attributed to the detrimental impact of air pollution, and that indoor air pollution is a more significant risk to children worldwide than outdoor air pollution [N7-R1]. These findings are consistent with regional variation because poverty and air pollution are often geographically uneven across Ethiopia.

The evidence also points to specific regional risk factors. A study from Jigjiga city, Somali region, Ethiopia, found that children carried on their mothers’ backs during cooking, had a history of household acute respiratory infection, were partially vaccinated, unvaccinated, had diarrhea, or were female, all of which were significantly associated with under-five pneumonia [N6-F3]. This regional study provides a concrete example of how risk factors can differ by setting: cooking smoke exposure, household respiratory infection, and vaccination status were all important. Another study from Awi Zone, Northwest Ethiopia, aimed to assess community-acquired pneumonia and its associated factors among under-five children, but the excerpt does not provide the full risk factor results [N4-R3]. The evidence on determinants of pneumonia among under-five children in Ethiopia therefore shows that regional studies can identify different combinations of risk factors, even within the same age group [N6-F3].

The evidence also indicates that severity and outcomes differ by region and by setting. A study on severe pneumonia outcomes among children aged 2 months to 59 months at Jimma University Specialized Hospital reported that risk factors for poor outcome included rural residence, poor infrastructure, parental literacy, vaccination, nutrition, and other clinical factors [N7-R3]. This suggests that severity and outcomes are not only determined by infection itself but also by the healthcare environment and socioeconomic conditions in the region. Another study on recovery time from severe community-acquired pneumonia noted that age, vaccination status, presence of danger signs, comorbidities, and duration of illness were important predictors of recovery time [N7-R4]. These findings support the idea that outcomes vary by region because the study populations differ in access to care, vaccination coverage, and underlying health status.

Limitations in interpreting regional risk patterns are considerable. First, the studies are heterogeneous: some are population-based surveys, others are hospital-based, and some are regional cohort studies [N6-F3][N4-R3][N7-R3]. This heterogeneity makes direct comparison of risk factors difficult. Second, the evidence suggests that the same risk factor can be important in different ways across regions. For example, indoor air pollution is a major risk factor in Ethiopia overall, but the specific exposures that matter may differ by region, such as cooking smoke versus other pollutants [N7-R1]. Third, the evidence indicates that outcomes such as recovery time and poor outcome are influenced by factors like vaccination status, parental literacy, and infrastructure, which are themselves regionally uneven [N7-R3][N7-R4]. Fourth, the evidence is limited by the fact that not all regional studies report the full set of risk factors or outcome measures, so some variation may be underappreciated or overestimated [N4-R3].

Overall, the evidence supports a cautious but meaningful conclusion: regional variation in pneumonia risk factors and severity exists in Ethiopia, with some regions emphasizing poverty, indoor air pollution, and household exposure, while others emphasize vaccination status, parental literacy, and infrastructure [N7-R1][N6-F3][N7-R3]. However, the available evidence is not uniform across regions, and the risk patterns should be interpreted with caution because the studies differ in design, setting, and outcome measures [N6-F3][N4-R3][N7-R3].

## Overall conclusion

The evidence from the included studies supports a clear conclusion: in Ethiopia, **reported prevalence rates of bacterial pneumonia and multidrug resistance (MDR) vary substantially across regions, but the variation is not uniform and is heavily influenced by study design, age group, setting, and pathogen type** [N1-F1][N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. The regional differences are real, but they must be interpreted cautiously because the studies differ in diagnostic methods, sampling settings, and outcome measures, which limits direct comparison [N1-F1][N5-F2][N6-F3][N11].

## Regional variation in bacterial pneumonia prevalence

The branch report on regional pneumonia prevalence shows that Ethiopia is not a single homogeneous setting. A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that the pooled prevalence of bacterial pneumonia in Ethiopia was 37.17% (95% CI 25.72–46.62), but the individual studies in that review reported a wide range from 6.19% to 46.3% [N1-F1][N1-R1]. This wide range implies that prevalence can differ substantially across regions and studies.

The evidence also indicates that regional prevalence differs by age group and setting. The same review noted that the positive culture rate was slightly higher in women and that higher prevalence rates were observed in age groups greater than or equal to 45 years [N1-F1]. In other words, prevalence is not only regional but also age-dependent. The branch report also highlights that under-five children in Ethiopia had an overall pneumonia prevalence of 20.68% in a systematic meta-analysis, with a wide range from 4.1% to 39.6% [N1-R4]. This reinforces that prevalence varies by region, by age group, and by study population.

The branch report further notes that specific regional studies exist in Ethiopia. For example, a study from Jigjiga city, Somali region, Ethiopia, reported a pneumonia prevalence of 33.4% among under-five children [N6-F3]. Another regional study in Wondo Genet district, Sidama Zone, Ethiopia, focused on children aged 2–59 months [N6-R3]. In hospitalized adult pneumonia studies, one regional study reported that bacterial pathogens were verified in 50% of sputum samples, with Klebsiella species as the most common isolate [N5-F2]. These examples show that prevalence varies by region and by setting, with outpatient, hospitalized, and community studies producing different estimates.

## Confidence in regional estimates and study limitations

Confidence in regional estimates is limited by substantial heterogeneity and study design differences. The bacterial pneumonia meta-analysis had I² = 98.4%, indicating very high heterogeneity across studies [N1-F1]. This means that regional comparisons are not straightforward and that the same region can appear very different depending on the study population and methodology [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The branch report on study comparability and regional bias also notes that diagnostic methods differ across studies, including direct microbiological testing, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses of observational studies [N11]. This further reduces comparability.

Sampling bias is another important limitation. The evidence includes studies from Addis Ababa, Dessie, southwest Ethiopia, and Jigjiga city in the Somali region [N1-R1][N5-F2][N6-F3]. These locations differ in urban/rural setting and in the care environment. The southwest Ethiopia study was conducted at a teaching and referral hospital in Jimma, which serves a large catchment population and is therefore likely to include more severe or hospitalized cases [N5-F2]. In contrast, the Jigjiga study was conducted in public hospitals and focused on outpatient departments [N6-F3]. A study from Awi Zone, Northwest Ethiopia, also focused on under-five children in a regional setting [N4-R3]. These differences in setting mean that prevalence may reflect different populations and different disease severity distributions.

## Multidrug resistance and resistance patterns

The branch report on multidrug resistance and resistance patterns shows that MDR is common among Ethiopian pneumonia-associated bacteria. The pooled prevalence of MDR in bacteria isolated from patients with pneumonia in Ethiopia was 67.73% (95% CI: 57.05–78.40) [N2-R1]. A separate systematic review of Ethiopia-wide MDR prevalence found an overall pooled prevalence of 70.5%, with Sidama region at the highest reported MDR level (81.7%) and Tigray at the lowest (51.1%) [N2-R2]. These regional differences suggest that MDR prevalence is not uniform across Ethiopia and may vary substantially depending on the local study population.

The evidence also shows that multidrug resistance is not confined to one region or one pathogen type. The systematic review and meta-analysis reported that the most commonly isolated bacteria were Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae, with Klebsiella pneumoniae having the highest pooled prevalence at 21.97% (95% CI 16.11–27.83) and Streptococcus pneumoniae at 17.02% (95% CI 9.19–24.86) [N1-F1]. The review explicitly notes that multidrug resistance is especially notable for the most common causative agents of pneumonia in Ethiopia, and that these organisms have developed high MDR in recent decades [N1-F1]. This means that resistance patterns are pathogen-specific and likely region-specific.

On resistance genes and patterns, the evidence is thinner and more indirect than the prevalence estimates. However, the evidence does not provide a full catalog of resistance genes across all regions; the regional differences reported are mainly in prevalence rather than in gene-level details.

## Regional variation in risk factors and severity

The branch report on regional variation in risk factors and severity shows that risk factors for pneumonia and pneumonia outcomes vary by region in Ethiopia. The evidence notes that pneumonia deaths are strongly linked to poverty-related factors, including inadequate nutrition, lack of access to safe water and sanitation, indoor air pollution, and limited healthcare access [N7-R1]. It also emphasizes that almost half of all pneumonia deaths can be attributed to air pollution, and that indoor air pollution poses a more significant risk to children worldwide than outdoor air pollution [N7-R1]. These findings support the idea that regional variation is real, but the specific exposures that matter may differ by region.

One regional example comes from Jigjiga city, Somali region, Ethiopia, where children carried on their mothers’ backs during cooking, had a history of household acute respiratory infection, were partially vaccinated, unvaccinated, had diarrhea, or were female, all of which were significantly associated with under-five pneumonia [N6-F3]. This regional study provides a concrete example of how risk factors can differ by setting: cooking smoke exposure, household respiratory infection, and vaccination status were all important. The evidence also indicates that severity and outcomes differ by region and by setting. A study on severe pneumonia outcomes among children aged 2 months to 59 months at Jimma University Specialized Hospital reported that risk factors for poor outcome included rural residence, poor infrastructure, parental literacy, vaccination, nutrition, and other clinical factors [N7-R3]. Another study on recovery time from severe community-acquired pneumonia noted that age, vaccination status, presence of danger signs, comorbidities, and duration of illness were important predictors of recovery time [N7-R4]. These findings support the idea that outcomes vary by region because the study populations differ in access to care, vaccination coverage, and underlying health status.

## Limitations in interpreting regional variation

The branch report on study comparability and regional bias highlights several important limitations. First, diagnostic methods differ across studies, which makes direct comparison difficult. Some studies used direct microbiological testing, others used systematic reviews or meta-analyses, and some studies used observational designs with different outcome measures [N11]. Second, sampling bias from urban versus rural or referral versus primary care settings is evident. The evidence includes studies from Addis Ababa, Dessie, southwest Ethiopia, and Jigjiga city in the Somali region, showing that prevalence can vary because hospitalized patients, outpatient children, and community settings may have different risk profiles and disease severity distributions [N1-R1][N5-F2][N6-F3]. Third, the wide prevalence range and high heterogeneity in bacterial pneumonia studies make it difficult to compare regional estimates directly [N1-F1][N1-R1].

## Synthesis

Taken together, the evidence supports the following integrated picture:

1. **Bacterial pneumonia prevalence varies substantially across Ethiopian regions**, with studies reporting a wide range from 6.19% to 46.3% [N1-R1][N1-F1].
2. **Regional differences are also evident by age group and setting**, with higher prevalence in older adults and women, and different prevalence in hospitalized adult studies versus under-five child studies [N1-F1][N5-F2][N6-F3].
3. **Multidrug resistance is common and regionally variable**, with pooled MDR prevalence around 67–70% nationally, but with regional contrasts such as Sidama at 81.7% and Tigray at 51.1% [N2-R1][N2-R2].
4. **Resistance patterns are pathogen-specific and likely region-specific**, with Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae as the main pathogens and multidrug resistance especially prevalent among them [N1-F1].
5. **Risk factors and severity also vary by region**, with poverty-related factors, indoor air pollution, cooking smoke, household respiratory infection, vaccination status, and infrastructure playing important roles [N7-R1][N6-F3][N7-R3].
6. **Interpretation is limited by study heterogeneity, diagnostic differences, and setting differences**, so regional estimates should be treated cautiously and compared only when studies are methodologically comparable [N1-F1][N11].

## Bottom line

In Ethiopia, the reported prevalence rates of bacterial pneumonia and multidrug resistance do vary across different regions, but the variation is not simply a uniform regional pattern. Instead, the evidence suggests that prevalence is influenced by age group, setting, and study design, while MDR is influenced by region, pathogen type, and resistance mechanisms such as ESBL and carbapenemase production [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2]. ## Overall conclusion

The evidence from the included studies supports a clear conclusion: in Ethiopia, **reported prevalence rates of bacterial pneumonia and multidrug resistance (MDR) vary substantially across regions, but the variation is not uniform and is heavily influenced by study design, age group, setting, and pathogen type** [N1-F1][N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. The regional differences are real, but they must be interpreted cautiously because the studies differ in diagnostic methods, sampling settings, and outcome measures, which limits direct comparison [N1-F1][N5-F2][N6-F3][N11].

## Regional variation in bacterial pneumonia prevalence

The branch report on regional pneumonia prevalence shows that Ethiopia is not a single homogeneous setting. A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that the pooled prevalence of bacterial pneumonia in Ethiopia was 37.17% (95% CI 25.72–46.62), but the individual studies in that review reported a wide range from 6.19% to 46.3% [N1-F1][N1-R1]. This wide range implies that prevalence can differ substantially across regions and studies.

The evidence also indicates that regional prevalence differs by age group and setting. The same review noted that the positive culture rate was slightly higher in women and that higher prevalence rates were observed in age groups greater than or equal to 45 years [N1-F1]. In other words, prevalence is not only regional but also age-dependent. The branch report also highlights that under-five children in Ethiopia had an overall pneumonia prevalence of 20.68% in a systematic meta-analysis, with a wide range from 4.1% to 39.6% [N1-R4]. This reinforces that prevalence varies by region, by age group, and by study population.

The branch report further notes that specific regional studies exist in Ethiopia. For example, a study from Jigjiga city, Somali region, Ethiopia, reported a pneumonia prevalence of 33.4% among under-five children [N6-F3]. Another regional study in Wondo Genet district, Sidama Zone, Ethiopia, focused on children aged 2–59 months [N6-R3]. In hospitalized adult pneumonia studies, one regional study reported that bacterial pathogens were verified in 50% of sputum samples, with Klebsiella species as the most common isolate [N5-F2]. These examples show that prevalence varies by region and by setting, with outpatient, hospitalized, and community studies producing different estimates.

## Confidence in regional estimates and study limitations

Confidence in regional estimates is limited by substantial heterogeneity and study design differences. The bacterial pneumonia meta-analysis had I² = 98.4%, indicating very high heterogeneity across studies [N1-F1]. This means that regional comparisons are not straightforward and that the same region can appear very different depending on the study population and methodology [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The branch report on study comparability and regional bias also notes that diagnostic methods differ across studies, including direct microbiological testing, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses of observational studies [N11]. This further reduces comparability.

Sampling bias is another important limitation. The evidence includes studies from Addis Ababa, Dessie, southwest Ethiopia, and Jigjiga city in the Somali region [N1-R1][N5-F2][N6-F3]. These locations differ in urban/rural setting and in the care environment. The southwest Ethiopia study was conducted at a teaching and referral hospital in Jimma, which serves a large catchment population and is therefore likely to include more severe or hospitalized cases [N5-F2]. In contrast, the Jigjiga study was conducted in public hospitals and focused on outpatient departments [N6-F3]. A study from Awi Zone, Northwest Ethiopia, also focused on under-five children in a regional setting [N4-R3]. These differences in setting mean that prevalence may reflect different populations and different disease severity distributions.

## Multidrug resistance and resistance patterns

The branch report on multidrug resistance and resistance patterns shows that MDR is common among Ethiopian pneumonia-associated bacteria. The pooled prevalence of MDR in bacteria isolated from patients with pneumonia in Ethiopia was 67.73% (95% CI: 57.05–78.40) [N2-R1]. A separate systematic review of Ethiopia-wide MDR prevalence found an overall pooled prevalence of 70.5%, with Sidama region at the highest reported MDR level (81.7%) and Tigray at the lowest (51.1%) [N2-R2]. These regional differences suggest that MDR prevalence is not uniform across Ethiopia and may vary substantially depending on the local study population.

The evidence also shows that multidrug resistance is not confined to one region or one pathogen type. The systematic review and meta-analysis reported that the most commonly isolated bacteria were Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae, with Klebsiella pneumoniae having the highest pooled prevalence at 21.97% (95% CI 16.11–27.83) and Streptococcus pneumoniae at 17.02% (95% CI 9.19–24.86) [N1-F1]. The review explicitly notes that multidrug resistance is especially notable for the most common causative agents of pneumonia in Ethiopia, and that these organisms have developed high MDR in recent decades [N1-F1]. This means that resistance patterns are pathogen-specific and likely region-specific.

On resistance genes and patterns, the evidence is thinner and more indirect than the prevalence estimates. The strongest direct evidence is that multidrug resistance is defined as resistance to at least three or more classes of antibiotics, and the review explicitly notes the presence of extensive drug resistance (XDR) and pan-drug resistance (PDR) as more extreme forms of resistance [N1-F1]. A separate regional study from southwest Ethiopia reported that 77.5% of isolates were multidrug resistant, with 40.5% ESBL producers and 10.8% carbapenemase producers [N5-F2]. This regional study provides a concrete example of resistance patterns: carbapenemase and extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) production are both important resistance mechanisms, and their co-occurrence is associated with very high MDR levels [N5-F2]. However, the evidence does not provide a full catalog of resistance genes across all regions; the regional differences reported are mainly in prevalence rather than in gene-level details.

## Regional variation in risk factors and severity

The branch report on regional variation in risk factors and severity shows that risk factors for pneumonia and pneumonia outcomes vary by region in Ethiopia. The evidence notes that pneumonia deaths are strongly linked to poverty-related factors, including inadequate nutrition, lack of access to safe water and sanitation, indoor air pollution, and limited healthcare access [N7-R1]. It also emphasizes that almost half of all pneumonia deaths can be attributed to air pollution, and that indoor air pollution poses a more significant risk to children worldwide than outdoor air pollution [N7-R1]. These findings support the idea that regional variation is real, but the specific exposures that matter may differ by region.

One regional example comes from Jigjiga city, Somali region, Ethiopia, where children carried on their mothers’ backs during cooking, had a history of household acute respiratory infection, were partially vaccinated, unvaccinated, had diarrhea, or were female, all of which were significantly associated with under-five pneumonia [N6-F3]. This regional study provides a concrete example of how risk factors can differ by setting: cooking smoke exposure, household respiratory infection, and vaccination status were all important. The evidence also indicates that severity and outcomes differ by region and by setting. A study on severe pneumonia outcomes among children aged 2 months to 59 months at Jimma University Specialized Hospital reported that risk factors for poor outcome included rural residence, poor infrastructure, parental literacy, vaccination, nutrition, and other clinical factors [N7-R3]. Another study on recovery time from severe community-acquired pneumonia noted that age, vaccination status, presence of danger signs, comorbidities, and duration of illness were important predictors of recovery time [N7-R4]. These findings support the idea that outcomes vary by region because the study populations differ in access to care, vaccination coverage, and underlying health status.

## Limitations in interpreting regional variation

The branch report on study comparability and regional bias highlights several important limitations. First, diagnostic methods differ across studies, which makes direct comparison difficult. Some studies used direct microbiological testing, others used systematic reviews or meta-analyses, and some studies used observational designs with different outcome measures [N11]. Second, sampling bias from urban versus rural or referral versus primary care settings is evident. The evidence includes studies from Addis Ababa, Dessie, southwest Ethiopia, and Jigjiga city in the Somali region, showing that prevalence can vary because hospitalized patients, outpatient children, and community settings may have different risk profiles and disease severity distributions [N1-R1][N5-F2][N6-F3]. Third, the wide prevalence range and high heterogeneity in bacterial pneumonia studies make it difficult to compare regional estimates directly [N1-F1][N1-R1].

## Synthesis

Taken together, the evidence supports the following integrated picture:

1. **Bacterial pneumonia prevalence varies substantially across Ethiopian regions**, with studies reporting a wide range from 6.19% to 46.3% [N1-R1][N1-F1].
2. **Regional differences are also evident by age group and setting**, with higher prevalence in older adults and women, and different prevalence in hospitalized adult studies versus under-five child studies [N1-F1][N5-F2][N6-F3].
3. **Multidrug resistance is common and regionally variable**, with pooled MDR prevalence around 67–70% nationally, but with regional contrasts such as Sidama at 81.7% and Tigray at 51.1% [N2-R1][N2-R2].
4. **Resistance patterns are pathogen-specific and likely region-specific**, with Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae as the main pathogens and multidrug resistance especially prevalent among them [N1-F1].
5. **Risk factors and severity also vary by region**, with poverty-related factors, indoor air pollution, cooking smoke, household respiratory infection, vaccination status, and infrastructure playing important roles [N7-R1][N6-F3][N7-R3].
6. **Interpretation is limited by study heterogeneity, diagnostic differences, and setting differences**, so regional estimates should be treated cautiously and compared only when studies are methodologically comparable [N1-F1][N11].

## Bottom line

In Ethiopia, the reported prevalence rates of bacterial pneumonia and multidrug resistance do vary across different regions, but the variation is not simply a uniform regional pattern. Instead, the evidence suggests that prevalence is influenced by age group, setting, and study design, while MDR is influenced by region, pathogen type, and resistance mechanisms such as ESBL and carbapenemase production [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2]. The studies are also heterogeneous, so direct comparisons should be made with caution [N1-F1][N11].
